Lessons.Title: Graphing from the Factored Form
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: graph a quadratic using factors to find zeros, use sign and symmetry to determine opening and vertex, and verify intercepts via substitution. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U06:L11 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/6/11/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/6/11/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source specifically asks students to check the zero-factor-to-intercept connection.

Original function g(x)=−2(x−1)(x−5). Its zeros are1 and5, axis of symmetry x3. At x3 the two factors are2 and−2, so g(3)=−2×(−4)=8, a maximum because leading coefficient is negative. At x0, g(0)=−2(−1)(−5)=−10, the y-intercept.

Additional symmetric values g(2)=−2(1)(−3)=6 and g(4)=−2(3)(−1)=6. The graph opens downward and lies above horizontal axis between zeros but below outside them. Plot points (0,−10),(1,0),(2,6),(3,8),(4,6),(5,0),(6,−10) on common axes.

For the comparison, h(x)=+2(x-1)(x-5) has the same zero-factor inputs x=1 and x=5 as g, but vertex (3,-8) and y-intercept (0,10). Unlike g, it opens upward. This second independently constructed function is an original analogous task rather than a copy of the publisher activity.

Student task (original first-party source-equivalent comparison): without reading the prepared graph first, use g(x)=-2(x-1)(x-5) and h(x)=2(x-1)(x-5) to predict BOTH x-intercepts, each vertex, and each y-intercept. Complete an original table at x=0,1,2,3,4,5,6 for both functions. Plot the two parabolas on the SAME labeled coordinate axes, with distinct colors or point markers. Justify why their x-intercepts agree but their opening, extrema and y-intercepts differ; verify predictions using graphing technology if available. Submit your own plotted graph plus reasoning to an authorized teacher. A pre-drawn SVG is only an explanatory example, not an auto-graded student submission. Human-reviewed draft rubric: 0–2 each for correct table/zero products, both graphs with scale and labels, vertex/y-intercept reasoning, and actual independent verification and explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Zero-product graph rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: Zeros occur where at least one displayed factor vanishes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Leading-coefficient sign
KeyConcepts.Definition: Negative a gives downward opening with maximum vertex.

KeyConcepts.Title: Axis between zeros
KeyConcepts.Definition: The vertex lies midway between distinct roots of a quadratic.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find all intercepts

Steps: First factor zero at1; second zero at5.

This confirms positive between zeros and negative outside.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using factor constants with same sign for roots
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Solve factor equal zero, reversing the sign inside.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a negative coefficient makes all outputs negative
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Quadratic may be positive between roots.

SummaryPoints: Factored form makes horizontal intercepts directly accessible.
Negative leading coefficient makes the quadratic open downward.
Teacher reviews labelled graph and sign reasoning.
